newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fed tightening to stop at FF rate of 6.0% -- UBS.
newsitem.headline: Fed tightening to stop at FF rate of 6.0% -- UBS.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve's current round of monetary tightening will end when its Federal funds (FF) rate reaches six percent, compared with 5.5 percent at present, an economist at UBS Securities predicted on Wednesday.

"The Fed has started the process of moving from neutral to restrictive. That process started at 5-1/4 percent for the Fed funds rate and we think that process will end at six percent," Paul McCulley, New York-based managing director and chief economist at UBS Securities LLC, told a seminar in Tokyo.
He noted that economic growth in the United States in the last two quarters had averaged about four percent while the consumer price index (CPI) had been flat.
"The continuation of four percent growth will raise the risk of inflation," he said.
McCulley said the Fed did not need to tighten very much from the current level as the credit tightening had been conducted with appropriate timing.
He added that the level of economic growth and inflation had been well controlled.
On March 25, the Fed decided to raise the FF rate by 25 basis points to 5.5 percent. This was the first rate increase in more than two years.
"(This year) is not 1994...Six percent is the number that would be respected and that's what we have to deal with," McCulley said.
Assuming the FF rate would be capped at 6.0 percent, McCulley forecast the target level of the yield of the key two-year Treasury note at 6-3/4 percent and the key 30-year bond at 7-1/4 percent.
"I'm short myself. I will cover and go long at 6-3/4 for the two-year note and for the long bond 7-1/4 is the target to cover my short," he said.
The two-year Treasury note yield was at 6.44 percent and the 30-year bond yield at 7.05 percent in late Asian trade on Wednesday. -- Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3-3432-8785
